speechtext:
There is a Canadian Press despatch reproduced pretty generally in the press which I think demands a word of explanation if not also of comment. It is published in this morning's Citizen under the following title:
Blame Premier for Empire Day sitting: Dominion convention of the Orange Young Britons passes resolution.
The despatch is dated Peterboro, Ontario, May 26, and reads:
The following resolution was unanimously passed by the Dominion convention of Orange Young Britons in session here to-day:
Whereas the House of Commons of Canada adjourned on Ascension Day, a Roman Catholic holiday, and on the direction of the Prime Minister of Canada the same House of Commons sat yesterday, May 25, the day set apart for the commemoration of Her Gracious Majesty Queen Victoria, be it resolved that this grand lodge of Orange Young Britons place itself on record as condemning the unpatriotic and unprotestant attitude of the Prime Minister of Canada in thus permitting the Roman Catholic hierarchy to control and dictate his actions which violate every principle of British imperialism and a free Canadian government.
So far as the House not sitting on Ascension Day is concerned, parliament on this occasion has but followed the practice which has been observed from the days of confederation up to the present time, implementing a pledge given in this House directly with respect to the employment of civil servants and indirectly with respect to the sitting of the House of Commons itself on that day. The pledge to which I refer was given by the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden when he stood in the position which, at the moment, I occupy. If hon. members will refer to Hansard of June 26, 1920, at page 4262, they will find the record of a discussion which took place in this House at that time with reference to the observance of certain religious holidays. Speak-

ing particularly of Ascension Day as one of those holidays, the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden is reported as follows:
I have said two or three times that so far as these days of religious observance and religious duty are concerned, the whole matter has rested on custom and convention.
A little further on he says:
I hope hon. gentlemen will accept the assurance on behalf of the government that this custom and convention which has prevailed in the past will continue in the future.
I think my right hon. friend opposite (Mr. Meighen) when he was Prime Minister followed the same practice in asking the House to refrain from sitting on Ascension Day, as being a day of religious observance so far as a large number of hon. members of the House are concerned, and in accordance with the custom which had prevailed, I understand, from the days of confederation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
But I am also referring to V ictoria Day, Mr. Speaker; the article has reference to both. I would respectfully submit that there is not a phrase in the explanation I have so far given the House that is not essential to a proper statement of the government's action in this matter. With regard to the sitting of the House on Victoria Day, I took the trouble of communicating with the High Commissioner for Canada to ascertain what the practice of the British government was with regard to the sitting of the British parliament on that particular day. I was informed that the British parliament would sit on Victoria Day and I felt that if the British parliament considered that a proper way to observe Victoria Day we should not be any less loyal if we observed the day in the same way. I should perhaps add that I had nothing to do with this House not sitting on Ascension Day; it was hon. members of the House of Commons themselves who, by unanimous resolution, agreed not to sit on that day. I merely brought before parliament a resolution to the effect that when the House adjourned on Wednesday, May 20, it should stand adjourned until Friday, the 22nd instant. That resolution was adopted unanimously by the House, so that it was the House itself that decided not to sit on Ascension Day. With respect to Victoria Day, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) asked:
What is the intention of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister with regard to sitting on Monday, May 25?
I replied, as reported at page 3168 of Hansard :
The government thought it would be meeting the wishes of the House generally if we sat on the 2oth May in order to get through the business as soon as possible.
No exception was taken to that statement; no hon. member asked that Victoria Day should be observed in any other manner than that indicated. Had there been any exception in any particular I would have told the House then, what I have just said, about the practice in the British House, and left it to the House itself to discuss the matter further.

The day was observed by the late government, and I repeat, I have no objection whatever to its observance at any time. As to Victoria Day, my understanding is-I speak subject to correction- that it is not a public holiday in England at all; it is in Canada. That distinction is worth drawing attention to.

speechtext:
Perhaps I might in a few
words outline the efforts that have been made internationally to limit or restrict the production of their drugs, especially at the last international conference at Geneva. The idea was to reduce the production of opium and the coca leaf to the medicinal and scientific requirements of the world. As was to be expected, strong objection was made to this proposal because, as can be understood, many interests are at stake in this connection.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: By what parties or nations were these objections to the restrictions made?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I was just coming to
that. The objections in some instances were qualified. There is an economic problem at the bottom of the whole question, arising out of the fact that a large number of peasants and agriculturists in various countries derive an income from the cultivation of the poppy in the case of opium, and the cultivation of the coca plant in the case of coca leaves. Probably millions of persons obtain a living through the cultivation of the -poppy in India, Persia, Turkey and China, and perhaps some other countries, and the cultivation of coca leaves in South America. In India opium is used in the form of what is called prepared opium-chiefly for mastication-which is entirely different from the opium used for smoking purposes, although British rule has during the last quarter of a century accomplished a great deal in restraining its use in that country. The idea prevails in India that some almost supernatural power attaches to opium; it is a family remedy which many of the natives of that country look upon as having the power to cure all ills, moral, mental or physical. So that if you prohibit the use

of prepared opium in India you meet with very serious objections on the part of people who claim that their individual liberty is being interfered with; that opium has come down to them from their ancestors and that the right to use it should by no means be taken from them.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister has put forward the idea that economic interests are the reason why the production of opium and its derivatives should not be interfered with in India. If the legislation which we are now considering, and which is to be paralleled in other countries, is effective, will it not have exactly the same result on the opium production in India as if it was prohibited at its source, and if Canada has a voice on the international board dealing with that matter, would it not be more effective to deal with it there than by legislating here?
Mr. BE'LAND:	We are mainly concerned
in Canada with the use of derivatives of these raw products I have mentioned. The derivatives are commonly known as salts. My hon. friend perhaps is aw*are that morphine, for instance is a derivative of opium, and so is codeine and heroin; cocaine and its salts are the derivatives of the coca leaves. I was dealing presently with the raw products, and I was about to mention that whilst opium is used as a chewing or masticating material in India, in China it is used for smoking purposes. There, again, you will run up against prejudices which are very deeply rooted in the minds of the population.
My hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg asked what was the use of making a law in this country to prohibit the use of narcotic drugs if you do not go to the very root of the question and stop production. Well, there is the difficulty, and it was that difficulty which caused the United States to withdraw from the conference at Geneva last winter. The United States submitted that all contracting parties should undertake to reduce the production of opium and coca leaves to the strictly medicinal and scientific requirements, and a limit of ten years was set by the United States. Very strong objections were taken to that by some countries, principally by Great Britain; not that Great Britain was willing to allow this evil to continue any longer than was necessary, but because of certain practical difficulties which were in the way. Hon. members will perhaps have noticed that Lord Robert Cecil at that conference submitted a proposal the sense of which was that Great 230

Britain would undertake to limit the production of opium in India and in any other British territory within ten years to run from the date when an international commission would certify that no contraband could take place from China. China is at the present time politically in a state of disorder; it is very unstable, and the illicit exportation of opium to other countries is very large. This proposal of the British delegation did not meet with the approval of the American representatives, who stuck to their proposal of doing away with the excess production of opium and coca leaves within ten years, claiming they had attained this end in the Philippine islands, which are under their administration.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Was it not two
years ago, on the initiation of Mr. Wellington Koo, Chinese representative on the council of the League of Nations, that the effort was made to prohibit the opium traffic in China, and was this effort not defeated by the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am not in a position to answer my hon. friend with any degree of accuracy in that connection. It is I think due to China that we should mention that as far back as 1908 the government of China undertook to pass legislation of a most drastic character in order to stop entirely the cultivation of the poppy. So drastic was this law that peasants who ran contraiy to it and indulged in the cultivation of the poppy were simply executed. That was shortly before the revolution in China, which did away entirely with those provisions. Since then other efforts have been made by other governments in China, but they have not amounted to very much. The country is so extensive and the population so immense that it must of necessity be very difficult to keep under strict control the contraband from China. So much for the problem which my hon. friend said we should deal with first.
The international conference has dealt with the traffic in opium and manufactured drugs as completely as is feasible under the circumstances. The conference in its convention provided for the creation of a central board of control, with its seat at Geneva, to be composed of eight members, of whom one will be appointed by the United States and one by Germany, and the other six by the League of Nations. Now the powers of that board are defined in a convention, and I do not suppose, Mr. Chairman, that you want me to go into very great detail in this connection. However, let me point out briefly that this board wili

Narcotic Drug Act

have the supervision of the world traffic in opium and coca leaves, and all derivatives of these two main raw products. Every contracting party-that is every party that has signed a convention

undertakes to submit to this central board before the end of each year an estimate of its medicinal and scientific requirements for the following year. That is the first condition. The second condition is that every contracting party will have to submit within three or five months after the end of each year the quantity of drugs, that is opium or coca leaves or drugs manufactured from these products, imported during the year within their territory, the quantity of drugs manufactured in their territory and the quantity of drugs consumed in their territory for medicinal and scientific purposes, the quantity left in stock, and the quantity exported. If this is done by every contracting party it is assumed that it will be possible for the central board to keep a close supervision of the traffic in drugs amongst the countries which are signatories to the convention. There is also a provision in the convention requiring an import and export license in the case of every import and every export. There is also a provision that every contracting party shall enact laws in order to control as closely as possible the mnufacture of drugs. Each manufacturer requiring a license to import must at any time be ready to allow his premises to be inspected by the governmental authorities in order to ascertain what quantity of the drug he has imported in a raw state or in a manufactured form, what quantity of the drug he has manufactured himself, what quantity he has disposed of, and what quantity remains in his possession. All these points have been covered very closely by the different committees of the conference. I think this explanation covers pretty well the subject which was raised by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg.

speechtext:
I should like to ask what attitude Canada took at this conference; whether this country through its representatives endorsed the attitude of Great Britain and the Indian delegates?
Mr. RELAND-: As far as Canada is concerned we are somewhat in the same position as the United States; we do not produce opium, we do not produce coca leaves, and we do not manufacture, to any great extent, any of these drugs. But in the last few days of the conference the representative of Canada, who during that time -was Mr. Riddell, agreed with Great Britain that the proposal of Lord Robert Cecil was acceptable. speechtext:
There are a few
remarks I should like to make. The minister has said that the production of opium is very extensive, and that it must not be interfered with on account of the welfare of the peasants of India. I should like to call attention to the fact that facing a deficit in 1923 the Inchcape Retrenchment committee report, after carefully considering the opium revenue, warns against any reduction of the price paid to cultivators, lest they turn to the growing of other crops and, to use the words of the report, that "this important source of revenue" will be endangered.
We must face the fact that very large financial interests are involved in this matter. 1 note that as late as 1923 the directors of the North Borneo Company acknowledge in their report a fear lest to introduce measures for the suppression of opium smoking would restrict the inflow of Chinese labour, which is "vital to the progress and development of North Borneo." Any check on a free flow of labour from China would have disastrous effects on the economic position of British Malaya.
And in their memorandum supplied to the conference, the Netherlands government offers the same excuse for the non-abolition for opium smoking in the Dutch East Indies. Foreign Affairs of November, 1923, states:

As long as large and important British colonies derive such a large percentage of their revenue from the production of opium, it is almost hopeless for us to attempt effectively to restrict the traffic. These bills that we discuss here and the penalties that we inflict upon local dealers in these drugs are very ineffective so long as we do not resolutely attack the main problem itself in the production and in the large revenues derived from the production of this commodity. It was stated as far back as 1891 by the British House of Commons that "the system by Which the Indian opium revenue is raised" is "morally indefensible." That statement still stands, and we in Canada ought to have sufficient courage to stand against that system, even though this may mean that in this regard, we must remain apart from some other portions of the British Empire.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Perhaps a word of explanation is in order. I do not think it is entirely fair-I say this in all due deference to my hon. friend-to convey to this committee the impression that the British government is deriving benefits out of the cultivation of the poppy.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not suggest anything

The matter is so regulated in India that each provincial government has complete control of whatever revenue there is. I am conveying to the committee only some information; which was given to the conference by the eminent, representative of India, Mr. Campbell. Mr. Campbell, in the face of forty-one representatives of the different nations of the
Narcotic Drug Act

world, stated emphatically that the government of India or the government of Great Britain did not derive a single cent from the cultivation of the poppy. If that was untrue, does my hon. friend not think that out of the forty other representatives there, objection might have been raised as to the accuracy of the affirmation of Mr. Campbell?
My hon. friend has said: Of what avail will it be to legislate in this country if we do not deal with the production of opium, especially in India? My hon. friend is, perhaps, not aware that not ten pounds of Indian opium are imported into the United States or Canada. The quality of opium raised in India is inferior, containing less than 5 per cent of alkaloids. The opium which is mainly used in the United States or in Europe for the manufacture of drugs is opium which is cultivated or raised in Persia and Turkey and which is a good deal richer in alkaloids than Indian opium. Therefore, even if we stopped entirely the cultivation of the poppy in India, that would not make any difference as regards America, because manufacturers in Europe would have their source of supply entirely in Persia and Turkey. I do not think my hon. friend is completely fair when he intimates that an immense revenue is derived by the British government from the cultivation of the poppy in India.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I did not say the British government. I said that the various colonies were deriving revenues from this traffic, not the British government itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is all right. No doubt in some of the provinces in India some revenue is derived from the cultivation of the poppy, and this may be true also of some other colonies of the empire in the Far East.
There is still this further objection in the way of those who want to suppress entirely the cultivation of the poppy. The conference was never animated by any desire to protect the revenue of any of those small countries, and I have not heard the British delegation or any delegation from the Orient claim that they should be protected as regards their revenue. Such a claim was never advanced during the conference. Some claims were made on behalf of the peasant cultivators, and some persons, such as the Persian representative, were of opinion that the big powers, the civilized nations, the European and American countries, should provide a means whereby those peasants could find a living if we stopped them from raising the poppy.

Mr. WOOiDSWORTH: Is it not true that Persia was willing to renounce any revenue which it might derive in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT

speechtext:

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT

This is an important

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT

way. And the illicit use of drugs is carried on to a very large extent in this way. I agree with the minister that the law against the use of narcotic drugs should be made as drastic as possible, but I think that everybody should be treated alike. I notice that section 5 amends section 6 of chapter 22 of the acts of 1923 and it deals specifically with physician-s. Now, in all cases of indictment there may be an appeal from the verdict of the jury to the Court of Appeal. That is all right. Brtt section 24 of the original act of 1922 provides under paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of section 4 that there shall be no appeal in the case of anyone importing into Canada or having in his possession any drug, without lawful authority, or of selling to a minor. There is no appeal in these particular cases. On the other hand, if a phj^sician sells drugs illegally or if he has drugs illegally in his possession and is prosecuted before a jury he may appeal. That is not dealing fairly as between one class and another; it is class legislation. Indeed, it is more than class legislation, inasmuch as the doctors of this country undoubtedly know much better than the man in the street who sells drugs the extent of the harm that may ensue. This refers also to cases tried before justices of the peace. An appeal may be taken from a judge and jury on questions of both law and fact, but if a magistrate tries certain cases defined-and sixty out of every hundred magistrates have no legal training-there is no appeal. My only object in bringing this to the minister's attention is to urge that we should have a uniform law for both the physician and the trafficker. But I do not think we can make *the law too drastic against those who deal illegally in drugs.

Anyone_who receives drugs from his physician must be treated by that physician in, the usual exercise of his profession. For instance, a man could not walk into a doctors office and receive a prescription for 100 grains of cocaine; it would be unlawful for the doctor to hand him such a prescription.
Replying to my hon. friend from Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll), I have already pointed: out the reason for the difference in the law. Usually, after securing his liberty by lodging an appeal, the trafficker disappears; but it is to be assumed that the regular practitioner has a well-established place for carrying on his profession, and it would be an exception indeed for him to run away. Of course, in the administration of this act a good deal of discretion must be exercised. It sometimes happens that a physician prescribes narcotic drugs in such quantities as would lead one to believe he is doing so for an unlawful purpose, and in such cases proper care is exercised not to injure his reputation. It seems to me that we should have no mercy at all for the drug trafficker, many of whom are making immense fortunes from their illicit trade.

speechtext:
You are more merciful
to the doctor than to the trafficker.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We do not do that. I can assure my hon. friend that the department is very, very careful in those circumstances. speechtext:
I see the point raised by
my hon. friend. It is a very difficult matter to deal with. We may make the law as complete as we choose, but in the administration of it we find something lacking in its provisions. maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There is no increase in this item. The Department of Health, as the House is aware, is supposed to expand. It was created in 1919, and the first minister I think was the Hon. Mr. Rowell. At that time it was foreseen that the activities of the department would increase from year to year, but on account of financial conditions it has been the endeavour of my predecessor and myself to restrict as much as possible the expansion of the Department of Health. It is more or less a co-ordinating department, co-ordinating the activities which were previously carried on by the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Immigration and some other departments. The work that is carried on under the Food and Drugs Act is the combating of the adulteration of food and drugs, honey and maple products. Our inspectors secure samples from the dealers all over Canada and examine them, and see that the buying public is not defrauded.

As far as the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act is concerned, while we have the same administration, except perhaps that the supervision is more strict, our activities in this regard are perhaps increased, though we do not ask for any more money. During the course of last year we think we have performed some good work in the suppression of the illicit traffic in drugs. It is a difficult problem to deal with inasmuch as the narcotic drugs which are smuggled into this country and sold illicitly can !be earned in a very small compass indeed.	*
As far as the Proprietary or Patent Medicines Act is concerned, we issue licenses, and we derive some revenue from that source, also some revenue under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, and under the Food and Drugs Act administration. This branch is not self-sustaining, but a substantial revenue is derived. A proprietary medicine is a medicine which carries its own formula. It is not required to be licensed as does a patent medicine inasmuch as t'he formula of that medicine is supposed to be a secret. The department is in possession of the patent medicine formula, however, and submits it to its advisory board which board decides whether the sale of the medicine can be permitted without harm to the public. Proprietary medicines, of course, must otherwise comply with the provisions of the act. The amount is the same as last year.

There is an increase under this heading of $20,000. The purpose of this vote is to defray all expenditure incurred in connection with the treatment of sick and deceased mariners, in conformity
5 p.m. with the provisions of part 5, chapter 113, Canada Shipping Act. It comprises the maintenance of marine hospitals owned by the government of Canada, salaries to medical officers; board and medical and surgical treatment of seamen at local and designated hospitals; grants to seamen's institutes, and so forth. The department operates two marine hospitals, one at Sydney and the other at Lunenburg. At other ports provision is made as far as possible for the treatment of sick sailors at contract rates at various local hospitals. Where there is no marine or designated hospital, provision is made for their treatment at private residences, in some instances, or public boarding houses. The expenditure is generally approximately the same as the revenue derived from the collection of sick mariners' dues. The dues are two cents per ton for every call of the ship, as long as the ship in question does not call more than three times a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is perfectly obvious to me that over a period of years, including last year, the collections on the Pacific coast have been out of all proportion to the expenditure, and in view of the representations that have been made from time to time it seems to me that a solution should now be attempted. Various organizations on the Pacific coast have made concrete suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend to give him some information which has been handed to me? I think it might be of interest to him. This is a statement from 1919-20 to 1924-25 .showing the net expenditure and the net surplus or deficit for Vancouver. I will give simp'y the last three years. The net revenue for 1922-23 was $26,213 and the net surplus $5,888. In 1923-24 the net revenue was $37,211 and the net surplus $21,420. In 1924-25 the net revenue was $32,193, net expenditure $27,781 and the net surplus $4,411.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have no doubt that in certain years the expenditures have been larger than others, but if the minister will take a period of ten years he will find that the average paid on the Pacific is out of all proportion to that paid on the Atlantic. He might well amend the law so as to ensure that the same proportion will be paid in respect to ships calling at the Pacific ports as at Atlantic ports. I take it that more ships come to Montreal from foreign ports than come to Vancouver.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: The number must be larger, I should say.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
And the tonnage must be greater as well. Yet for the whole of Quebec the total collections were only $46,000, whereas in British Columbia the amount was $64,511 for the same year. It is true it is for the whole year round, but that does not alter the fact that even for the short season there are more ships and greater tonnage from foreign ports calling at Quebec ports than at British Columbia ports.
Mr. BELAND Month by month, yes.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: During the whole period of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: For the year? I do not think so.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think I am correct. I suggest that the minister average it up over a period of years and make an adjustment of the tax so that ships which can only make a limited number of calls in a year and can only obtain a limited service will pay rate-ably the same as foreign ships that come to the eastern ports. A very simple amendment would meet that situation and bring satisfaction to the Pacific coast on this matter. They have been exercised over it for many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I will undertake to look into it further and see what can be done.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
How many mariners
are treated in these hospitals at the various ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I can give the total number. The information as to ports can no doubt be easily obtained from the Auditor General's report. The number of seamen treated in one year was 2,745.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I notice in the Auditor General's report that there are quite a number of physicians at the various ports in the employ of the government to look after these seamen. Would the minister give their names and salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We have in every port
what we call a port physician. Unlike other employees of the government, the port physicians receive a very small remuneration. We have a long list of port physicians in Nova Scotia, the salary ranging from $150 to $400 per annum, for the most part, there is one who receives $1,300, and one at $550. But they are all small salaries. Of course many of them are not called frequently to treat seamen, but this is given them as a retaining fee. In New Brunswick the salaries range from $150 to $600, and in Prince Edward Island from $100 to $400. In Quebec there
Supply-Health

are six, receiving salaries from $300 to $450, and in British Columbia three, receiving $600, $600 and $400 respectively.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am rather surprised at the number of physicians in the employ of the government. What are their duties? They must be mostly in small ports where there is no sea-going trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: They go on board all vessels that call at the port and any seaman who requires treatment may get it from the port physician. A sick seaman is taken to hospital if necessary, and for that service we pay a flat rate per day. If there is no hospital he is taken to a boarding house or a private residence.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: That would be in connection with coastal trade, not trans-Atlantic trade, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, the small vessels are eligible.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: You have none of that character on the Great Lakes, in the boundary waters there.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I did not expect to find there were so many physicians in the small ports in the pay of the government. I was more interested in the pay of those in the larger ports, Halifax, St. John, Quebec and Montreal. I should like to know the physicians who are at these four ports, and what their salaries are.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: The seamen in these ports are sent to the hospital, and we have a rate with the hospital which includes medical attendance from the hospital physicians and surgeons in those ports.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Has there been a change made in the act recently? The last Auditor General's report shows that the physicians in these various harbours are in the pay of the government, and I presumed they were on annual pay.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Those are quarantine
officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Those are different.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am not objecting to the two hospitals at all. They may be quite necessary. I know nothing about the conditions, but I do know that hospitals now are very expensive. You maintain and equip a marine hospital at Sydney. Is there a necessity for that .now that you have general hospitals where these men can be taken care of, without maintaining special hospitals?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I understand there were
a good many more hospitals than we have now. We have closed one marine hospital in Pictou, and one in Quebec was closed some years ago. We have only two left-, and these are maintained, I suppose, on account of the large number of fishermen who go to sea. It is optional for the shipowner to contribute the dues and have -their seamen treated at these hospitals.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am not objecting, but the minister knows as well as I do how costly.it is to maintain a hospital, and perhaps it is not as well to have two or three different kinds of hospitals in one place as to have one large one. I forgot quite about the necessity for the fishermen. Is that the particular reason for maintaining these two hospitals?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am informed that would be the reason.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Quarantine-salaries and contingencies of organized districts; Public Health in other districts; Tracadie and Bentinck Island Lazaret-toes, Leprosy generally and Public Works Health Act, $215,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There is a decrease of
$25,000 in this item, because we have made some changes, especially at. Quebec where we have been able to dispense with the cost of a boat plying between Grosse Isle and Quebec, as well as making some other retrenchments. We have moved all our minor cases to the city of Quebec, instead of treating them at Grosse Isle, where it was more expensive. The shipping companies have been advocating the change also on account of the fact that it does not delay the ships. As a matter of fact, I believe there was not a single .major case disembarked at Grosse Isle during last season; so the ships were not delayed at all. The appropriation provides for the maintenance of all quarantine stations, eight in number.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Could the minister give us some particulars regarding the lazaretto at Tracadie, more particularly as to the number of patients?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: There are now ten patients; we had eleven; one died during the year.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Did those cases originate locally?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There was one Chinaman
sent there from Montreal; the other cases,
I am informed originated in the maritime provinces.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would the minister
give us some information with regard to the quarantine facilities in Halifax and Quebec?

Supply-Health
What provision is made there for the receipt of the immigrants, and -what is done for the comfort of immigrants who are kept in quarantine?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The quarantine station
at Quebec is located on an island which is known as Grosse Isle, about twenty-five miles below the city of Quebec. It is an old station and is provided with all the facilities we would require for the treatment of major diseases. As I said, the minor cases are taken off the boat at Quebec and treated in some hospital there, thus saving some money, and saving a good deal of time to the ships. In some seasons the quarantine station at Grosse Isle is quite idle, but it is a necessity; we must have it. One ship may come in with ten major cases, and we may have to take off all the contacts there; we may have at one moment, without any notice at all, five hundred people on the island. We must thank God that does not happen, but if it did happen, and if we did not have the facilities for handling these cases the reputation of the whole country would suffer, and the government, whatever government was in power, would be open to very serious criticism. At Halifax the station is at Lawlor's Island. I have never visited it, but I understand that it is in the immediate vicinity of the port, and the same facilities are afforded there for the treatment of major cases.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: What are the prevailing infectious diseases brought in from Europe and elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The major diseases are
cholera, smallpox, typhus and yellow fever. We had not a single case at Grosse Isle during the last season of navigation. At Halifax there was one death at the hospital during the year-a child being held for deportation at the immigration building as a Mongol imbecile, developed chicken pojq was transferred to the quarantine hospital where it died of septicemia. One female passenger was detained for vaccination purposes.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: What number of infectious cases was treated at the quarantine hospital at St. John during the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
At St. John the station
is located on Partridge island. It is pretty well equipped but I grant the committee that the equipment could be better.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am asking for a
statement of the number of infectious cases treated during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am asking my official
to find that for me in the report. The figure is so small that it did not interest me as something that could be quoted except in a satisfactory manner.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman,
this i3 rather an important item. It is nearly six o'clock and I suggest that the item had better be held over.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend want
the vote for quarantine stations held over?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There are a few more
items to be passed, especially one for immigration medical inspection. I can assure hon. gentlemen that all information will be given on the items.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There are two or
three questions that arise in connection with the present vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am not objecting at all;
my only desire is to advance the work of the session. If my hon. friends wish this vote to be held, all right.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It is information
I am looking for.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT 1923 AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I want to give all possible information.
Progress reported.

Thursday, May 28, 1925.
